title: The Elohistic Psalter
lead: Psalms 42–83, the middle of the Psalter, call God Elohim ("God") far more often than by his name YHWH ("the LORD"). Most scholars think an editor changed the name in this collection; others think its singers simply preferred "God."

sections.b:
In Psalms 1–41 the name YHWH occurs about 278 times and the plain word elohim about 15. In Psalms 42–83 the proportions reverse: YHWH about 45 times, elohim about 200. Outside 42–83, in Psalms 84–150, YHWH again dominates. The block covers the Korah psalms 42–49, the Asaph psalm 50, the David psalms 51–72 and the Asaph psalms 73–83. The clearest evidence of an editor's hand is the doubled psalms: Psalm 53 is Psalm 14 with "God" wherever Psalm 14 has "the LORD" (14:2, 14:4, 14:7; the fourth falls in a rewritten verse), and Psalm 70 is Psalm 40:13–17 with similar changes. Phrases such as "God, your God" (Psalm 50:7; Psalm 45:7) and "O God, my God" (Psalm 43:4) look like replacements of "the LORD your God" and "O LORD my God."

Why the change was made is debated: reverence for the divine name (a step toward the later Jewish practice of not pronouncing it); the taste of one guild of singers; or a deliberate theological program stressing God as the God of all the earth. The collection itself was later joined to the David psalms of Book I and to Books III–V.
